question:
A unit hexagram is composed of a regular hexagon of side length \(1\) and its \(6\) equilateral triangular extensions, as shown in the diagram. What is the ratio of the area of the extensions to the area of the original hexagon?

[Figure 1](figures/2007_AMC_8_Q12_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The regular hexagon can be divided into triangles that match its extensions. Join its center to all six vertices. Regularity gives equal center-to-vertex lengths and six equal central angles, each measuring
\[
\frac{360^\circ}{6}=60^\circ.
\]
Each resulting triangle is isosceles with a \(60^\circ\) vertex angle, so its other two angles are also \(60^\circ\). Thus it is equilateral, with side length \(1\), just like each extension.

These six triangles fill the hexagon without overlapping interiors. Let \(t>0\) be the area of one equilateral triangle of side length \(1\). The extensions have total area \(6t\), and the original hexagon also has area \(6t\). Hence the requested ratio is
\[
6t:6t=1:1,
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\mathrm{A}}\).

reference.solution:
Method 1: Compare equal triangular pieces

The regular hexagon can be divided into triangles that match its extensions. Join its center to all six vertices. Regularity gives equal center-to-vertex lengths and six equal central angles, each measuring

edges.reason: Interior angle sums help with angle work. However, radius and apothem come from the central angle 360/n and a right triangle, and the interior angle follows from the central angle too.
The triangle circumcircle introduces circles through all vertices, which eases the generalization. Regular polygon center and radius can be defined via symmetry or equal division of a circle.

edges.reason: Classification usefully organizes varied examples and helps check that the angle-sum rule is not confined to one type. The same straight-angle rearrangement establishes the rule for an unclassified triangle, so the useful role is preparation rather than necessity.
edges.scope: Organizing empirical triangle angle-sum checks across acute, right and obtuse examples

edges.reason: Fraction division prepares ratio values with fractional terms. The target expressly permits a simple ratio, and a whole-number pair such as 6 to 3 needs only ordinary division; no fraction-by-fraction division is universal.
